questions.q: What is FAIR (Factor Analysis of Information Risk)?
options: A single-point dollar estimate any analyst can invent on the spot
A published, structured quantitative risk model, originally from Jack Jones, maintained by the FAIR Institute and also published as The Open Group's O-RA standard
A qualitative High/Medium/Low scoring matrix
A certification exam for security architects with no associated risk methodology
questions.explain: FAIR is a formal, published model with defined terms meant to be applied consistently across analysts — not an ad hoc label for "putting a dollar figure on something."

options: Risk = Likelihood x Impact, scored one to five
Risk = Number of findings x Average severity
Risk = Primary Loss x Secondary Loss only
Risk = Loss Event Frequency (LEF) x Loss Magnitude (LM)
questions.explain: FAIR's core equation is Loss Event Frequency multiplied by Loss Magnitude — each of which FAIR further decomposes into measurable sub-factors instead of asking for a direct guess.

questions.q: What is the difference between Threat Event Frequency (TEF) and Vulnerability in FAIR's decomposition of Loss Event Frequency?
options: TEF is how often an attacker attempts the action; Vulnerability is the probability that attempt actually succeeds given current controls
TEF and Vulnerability are two names for the exact same sub-factor
Vulnerability measures only software patch levels, unrelated to attacker behavior
TEF is measured in dollars, while Vulnerability is measured in hours of downtime
questions.explain: TEF counts how often a threat actor tries; Vulnerability is the probability a given attempt succeeds given the controls in place. Multiplying them gives Loss Event Frequency — how often a successful event is expected.

questions.q: Why does FAIR split Secondary Loss into Secondary Loss Event Frequency and Secondary Loss Magnitude?
options: Because regulators require exactly two sub-factors for every loss category
Because Primary Loss and Secondary Loss are otherwise mathematically identical
To separate how often a primary event actually triggers outside reactions from how large those reactions are when they do happen, since different experts and drivers estimate each one
Because Secondary Loss never actually occurs and the split is only theoretical
questions.explain: Not every breach triggers a lawsuit or regulatory fine. Splitting frequency from magnitude lets an analyst separately estimate how often secondary consequences happen and how big they are when they do, rather than conflating the two.

questions.q: Why does a FAIR analysis typically run ranges through Monte Carlo simulation instead of multiplying single-point estimates together?
options: Monte Carlo simulation is required by law for any security risk calculation
To produce a distribution of expected annual loss with a confidence interval, rather than collapsing loss into one misleading point score
Because FAIR cannot use real threat intelligence or loss history data
Single-point multiplication is actually forbidden under ISO 31000
questions.explain: Running estimated ranges through simulation produces a distribution, not a single number — directly addressing the problem from Lesson 9 where a single score hides the real shape of possible loss outcomes.
